data.name: Everything is going to be OK
data.detailed_description:
"Everything is going to be OK" is a desktop labyrinth of vignettes, poetry, strange fever dream games, and broken digital spaces. It is a collection of life experiences that are largely a commentary on struggle, survival, and coping with the aftermath of surviving bad things.
On the surface it comes across as dark comedy, and humor is a prevalent theme, but as you interact the themes start to unravel and facilitate a deeper discussion.

This is an anti-capitalist trauma-core 2D desktop-sim with clicker game action adventure elements based in an erratic cartoon world.
“Everything is going to be OK” features traditionally animated cartoons in eclectic worlds that you can explore. Everything is voice acted. In each space you interact with silly and distraught characters that you help survive or guide through reconciling with their fate. The circumstances are often humorous. It is a dark comedy about life.
There are hidden tangents, strange spaces, and lost digital worlds to uncover… all of which feature personal essays, fiction, and poetry hidden throughout. It includes a number of secret branching tangents in which you find silly artistic tools or cryptic toys that add to the humorous and often strange experience.
It is the type of game that is hard to describe and best experienced for yourself.
If you like fever-dreams, walking simulators, glitch art, arthouse games, alt games, or the absolute bizarre type of experimental play that leaves you both baffled and laughing… then this is for you.

"Everything is going to be OK" has appeared in a number of festivals, and publications... such as Game Developer, PC Gamer, Wired, Mashable... and winning IndieCade's Interaction Award, and AMAZE's Digital Moments. It was an IGF finalist for the Nuovo Award. It is also in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art, and was exhibited in Never Alone: Video Games and Other Interactive Design at the MoMA.

Sensitivity Warnings: This features bright flashy graphics and colors.
Mature themes are featured. Please respect the Content Rating and age-gate.
Difficult topics dealing with mental health and struggle are discussed.

reviews.review:
An interactive zine that plays with hypertextuality, straddling videogame, digital diary and glitch-art collage. Presented as a fake chaotic desktop inspired by early internet interfaces, it contains around 30 nonlinear pages of cartoon vignettes, poems, personal essays, public-domain footage, strange hidden tools, broken-looking programs and bizarre click-driven mini-games. Overlapping windows and glitchy visuals blur the boundary between fictional interface and real computer, with interactions allowing files to be exported and even connecting to Twitter.

The recurring white bunnies are the perfect introduction. They may be impaled, dismembered or set ablaze, yet insist they are coping, sometimes producing absurd motivational slogans as if suffering could become a shareable success story.

But beneath cute creatures, lurid and garish colours, glitch effects, sensory overload and dark humour lies a painfully personal question: how can suffering be communicated, and how should others respond when someone finally asks for help? Rather than simply presenting a cry for help, the game examines what such a plea might look like, and how pain must be expressed to become visible to others.

The cheery fatalism of the rabbits turns grotesque slapstick into a language for trauma, depression, anxiety, self-hatred, suicidal thoughts, strained relationships, dissociation and the exhausting pressure to appear okay.

Gradually, the game exposes the cruelty of empty reassurance, the way people recoil when someone admits they are hurting, and a culture that packages, performs or monetizes pain, turning it into an inspirational success story. A personal take on the power fantasy, radically redefining strength not as the ability to dominate others, but as the capacity to endure and overcome the harm they inflict. It condemns a culture that teaches people to remain perpetual survivors (to endlessly entertain others with a spectacle of resilience, reframing strength as continuing to live), rather than helping them heal. The game understands that sometimes laughter is all that remains when easy answers feel insulting.

There is no conventional plot or clear route to completion. The pages can be explored in almost any order. The mini-games constantly shift in form, often seeming deliberately futile; choices may barely matter, and the experience can turn the tables on you, making playing feel like a performance that the game itself observes and judges. The essays, poems and hidden fragments are often the real centrepiece.

Even the incessantly dismissive "weird game" streamer commentary becomes part of the critique of how videogames are denied serious artistic consideration. The game's sprawling, self-referential form can feel overwhelming, abrasive and occasionally typo-ridden, but the chaos is expressive, not random: the fractured interface embodies the difficulty of making pain legible. The work invites curiosity, but rewards attention more than mastery.

Part of MoMA's permanent collection, Everything is going to be OK is a strange, compassionate anti-capitalist art game: difficult, funny, painful and unexpectedly comforting. Beneath its confrontational grotesquerie lies an unusual sense of recognition for those who feel broken or rejected. It offers no easy cure or promise that everything will improve; instead, it suggests that life can remain painful and unresolved without losing its worth, finding dignity in coping and discovering small sparks of hope in the cracks. For all its nihilism, hostility and deliberately abrasive humour, the game ultimately holds on to the possibility of moving forward. Everything is not going to be OK, and that's OK.

8/10
